title: AI Prompts for HR Reporting: Dashboards & Cost Modeler
summary: Use AI to build a board-ready talent summary, dashboard, and HR cost calculator. Four copy-ready reporting prompts with PII and PHI guardrails.
body_markdown:
Most people leaders I know are sitting on more data than they can use. Headcount lives in the HRIS, spend lives in the ERP, hiring lives in the ATS, and the board wants one clear answer by Friday.


That is why reporting was the topic of our latest AI Prompts for HR session. A few months ago, OpenAI published economic research showing that only about 10% of the prompts HR professionals send to AI go toward HR work. We think that number is too low, and this series is our way of changing it.


Want to see the prompts run live or use our sample data?[Get the recording here.](https://warp.ondemand.goldcast.io/on-demand/266d568e-8584-4627-8527-34ab04d9c767)


## **How to write a reporting prompt that works**


Before the demos, a quick word on what makes a good prompt. Security and data handling matter (more on that below), but so does knowing what a good prompt even is. Every prompt in this guide uses the same five parts:


1. **Role and audience.** Tell the AI who you are and who the output is for. In the first example, I am the Head of People Analytics at a 120-person company writing for a board.
2. **The data.** Name the file and describe its shape: tabs, column names, conventions, and anything tricky. The better the data going in, the better the output.
3. **The structure.** Be specific about the format you want. I asked for a one-page board summary, not an essay and not a website.
4. **The audience level.** Spell out how plain the language should be. "Plain language a non-HR board member understands" changes the output more than you might think.
5. **The honesty clause.** Ask the AI to flag any number it is unsure about and to mark any conclusion that is an inference rather than something the data states. This is the most important part. It keeps the AI doing analysis, and keeps you making the decisions.


## **HR reporting prompts**


All four prompts use Kestrel Labs, a fictional 120 person company with 42 engineers, so about a third of the company sits on one team. I anonymized the data (department and manager names were swapped for codes like M1 and M11). Swap in your own files and numbers wherever you see a specific figure.


### **Prompt 1: A board-ready talent health summary**


The workbook has headcount, turnover, engagement surveys, engagement by tenure, engagement by manager, and exit data. This prompt turns all of it into a one-page summary a board member can read in two minutes.


> *You are the Head of People Analytics at a 120 person company. Using the attached workbook, write a one-page board summary on talent health. Structure it as: (1) a one-sentence headline, (2) the three biggest risks ranked by business impact, (3) trends versus the prior two quarters, (4) two recommended actions, each with an owner and a timeline. Use plain language a non-HR board member understands. For every number, name the tab it came from. Flag any number you are unsure about, and mark any conclusion that is an inference rather than something the data states directly.*


Three things make this work. The role and audience set the tone. The numbered structure keeps the output to one page. And the last two sentences are the honesty clause: naming the source tab for every number makes verification fast, and the inference label separates what the data says from what the AI is guessing.


The headline from our run: five departments looked healthy, but engineering was losing people and engagement was sliding. Engineering hires are some of the hardest and most expensive to make, so when a third of the company is destabilizing, that tells me where to focus first.


### **Prompt 2: Turn the summary into an interactive dashboard**


A long document is hard to share and hard to explore. So I turned the summary into something clickable.


> *Build this as an interactive board dashboard. Include a department filter, a quarter selector, voluntary attrition by quarter, engagement by tenure band, and the top three risks at the top. Board-ready styling. Use only the numbers in the workbook, do not invent any data. Confirm with me if you have questions or gaps to fill in.*


The key line is "use only the numbers in the workbook." It stops the AI from filling gaps with plausible-looking, but hallucinated, data. The last sentence also invites questions instead of guesses.


In about ten minutes, I had a dashboard with the top risks up front, attrition and engagement by band, and department and quarter filters. Filtering to engineering showed engagement falling from almost 4.0 to 3.7. Because I had given Claude our design system, it used our fonts and colors. I then shared a private link with my talent team and people ops team for a gut check on the numbers.


In the past, building a dashboard like this would have meant waiting on a designer or an engineer.


### **Prompt 3: HR cost efficiency analysis**


This one starts with a second workbook: recruiting and agency fees, software tools, benefits admin fees, quarter-over-quarter growth by function, time to fill and direct cost from the ATS, compliance costs including multi-state filings and outside accounting, plus headcount and HR hours.


> *Calculate HR cost per employee and cost per hire by quarter. Show the trend, tell me which one is moving in the wrong direction and why, and state how you defined each metric. Then identify the three largest drivers of HR cost growth over the six quarters in this data, with the dollar impact of each. Finally, rank where automation or process changes could reduce spend without hurting employee experience, by annual savings and by effort to implement. Separate hard cost savings from hours saved.*


I chose quarterly on purpose, because trends read as a story and a single month is just a data point. Asking the AI to state how it defined each metric means you can check the math. And separating hard savings from hours saved keeps you honest with finance.


The analysis pointed to the gap I would chase first. Total HR cost was growing, which is reasonable for a company that has grown headcount this much, and cost per employee was rising more slowly. But cost per hire was climbing much faster. The reason: agency hires went from about one in ten hires to four in ten. Two other drivers showed up. One software tool had nine active users but 120 paid seats, and manual payroll and tax admin hours more than doubled, from 60 hours a quarter to 110, as tax notices increased.


### **Prompt 4: Make it a calculator you can adjust live**


Analysis tells you what happened. A calculator lets you model what to do next.


> *Build an HR cost calculator I can adjust live. Inputs: headcount, hires per quarter, percent of hires from agencies, number of states we file in, and hours per week on payroll and tax admin. Outputs: HR cost per employee, cost per hire, annual spend, and a savings estimate if we shift agency hiring to referrals and automate filings. Include a bar chart comparing current and optimized. Use these assumptions from the data: $15,000 average agency fee, $3,000 referral bonus, 2 filings per state per quarter at $150 each, and 4 hours per tax notice. Label any other assumption you add. Do not invent numbers.*


The prompt gives the AI the assumptions from our own data, asks it to label any it adds, and repeats the "do not invent numbers" guardrail. The bar chart comparing current and optimized makes the result easy to explain to a CEO.


I used it to model our fictional CEO's ambitious plan to double from 120 to 240 people. Then I moved agency hiring toward referrals and sourcing, and the spend dropped. Then I automated tax filings and notices, and the calculator showed almost 500 hours a year saved. As always, I would check the assumptions with my internal teams before presenting any of it.


## **Is it safe to use AI for HR reporting?**


I get this question constantly, and it is the right one. People teams handle some of the most sensitive data in a company: PII, PHI, salaries. Here is how I think about it.


**Use an approved tool.** Check with your IT team on which AI tools are approved for your organization. At Warp, we are primarily a Claude shop and use an enterprise version, which comes with very different data guardrails.


**Anonymize when in doubt.** If you are conservative about it, and that is reasonable, input anonymized data. Instead of "Suzie May has XYZ salary," write "a person on my team has Y salary."


**Never let the AI make the decision.** AI is great at analyzing data, parsing research documents, and modeling scenarios. It is our job to take those outputs and decide what to do with them.


**Verify every number.** Before anything goes to the CEO or the board, check it. AI systems can hallucinate, and the accuracy of what you present is your responsibility. This is why every prompt above asks for source tabs and inference labels.
